concepts.def: A ranking of waste strategies where reducing consumption is most effective, followed by reusing products, then recycling materials into new feedstock.
Reprocessing waste material, for example melting down plastics or metals, into raw material for new products, reducing demand for virgin resources.
Designing products and services to deliver the same function using less material and energy, for example through miniaturisation or digital delivery.
Designing products so they can be taken apart easily at end of life, enabling repair, reuse of components and recovery of materials.
Energy from naturally replenished sources such as solar, wind and hydro, used in production to reduce dependence on fossil fuels.
Production methods designed to prevent pollution and waste being created at source, rather than treating them after they have occurred.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Resource Management & Sustainable Production — a core area of Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Resource Management & Sustainable Production brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Resource Management & Sustainable Production.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In the waste hierarchy, the most effective strategy is to:
options: Recycle as much material as possible
Reduce the resources consumed in the first place
Incinerate waste for energy
Export waste to other countries

mcqs.q: Design for disassembly makes a product more sustainable because it:
options: Allows easy separation of parts for repair, reuse and material recovery
Makes the product impossible to open
Increases the number of glued joints
Shortens the product's working life

mcqs.q: Which is the best example of dematerialisation?
options: Adding extra packaging layers for luxury appeal
Replacing printed manuals with a downloadable digital version
Using thicker steel than the design requires
Shipping products by air instead of sea

mcqs.q: Clean technology differs from end-of-pipe treatment because it:
options: Filters pollution after it leaves the factory
Ignores pollution completely
Prevents pollution and waste from being created at source
Only applies to water pollution

mcqs.q: What is the difference between reusing and recycling?
options: Yes - pollution can only ever be dealt with after it is created.
Reusing and recycling are two words for the same process.
Reuse keeps the product or component intact and uses it again; recycling destroys the product to reprocess its material into new feedstock, which consumes energy.
Recycling means selling a product second-hand.

mcqs.q: Is recycling cost-free for the environment?
options: Yes - pollution can only ever be dealt with after it is created.
No - collection, transport, sorting and reprocessing all consume energy and can create emissions; recycling is beneficial but not impact-free.
Yes - recycling generates energy rather than using it.
Yes - once material is recycled, its environmental impact is zero.

mcqs.q: Is treating pollution after production the best way to manage it?
options: Yes - filtering emissions at the chimney is the ideal solution.
No - clean technology aims to prevent pollution at source, which is generally cheaper and more effective than end-of-pipe treatment afterwards.
Recycling means selling a product second-hand.
Yes - pollution can only ever be dealt with after it is created.
